Verified
ver'-ī-fīd
v. (proved true; made good by the event)
Latin verus, true, and facere, to make — to make good, to show true. In the Authorized Version the word is used of words being proved by what happens, and twice it is the prayer that God's own word may be made good.

Biblical Definition

Joseph, unrecognized, sets his brothers a test: “bring your youngest brother unto me; so shall your words be verified, and ye shall not die. And they did so” (Gen 42:20). Their claim to be honest men would be proved not by protestation but by producing Benjamin — that is, by whether they would treat Rachel's other son as they had treated the first. Words are verified by events, and the whole of Genesis 42-45 is the working out of that single test, ending with Judah offering himself in the boy's place. The other two occurrences are the same sentence, prayed at the dedication of the temple: “And now, O God of Israel, let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father” (1Ki 8:26; 2Ch 6:17). Solomon has just built the house and has nothing to plead but a promise. That is the settled posture of biblical prayer — not asking God for something He has not said, but asking Him to make good what He has said. Every great prayer in Scripture does this: Moses at Sinai pleading the oath to Abraham, Daniel in Babylon reading the seventy years in Jeremiah and then praying them, our Lord teaching us to pray thy kingdom come.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines verify as to prove to be true, to confirm; and to fulfil, as a promise — citing the prayer that God's word may be verified.

expand to see more

VERIFY, v.t. To prove to be true; to confirm.

1. To fulfil, as a promise; to confirm the truth of a prediction; to show to be true.

VERIFIED, pp. Proved; confirmed; fulfilled.

VERITY, n. Truth; consonance of a statement, proposition or other thing to fact.

Key Scripture

1Ki 8:26 — "And now, O God of Israel, let thy word, I pray thee, be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David my father."

Gen 42:20 — "But bring your youngest brother unto me; so shall your words be verified, and ye shall not die. And they did so."

2Ch 6:17 — "Now then, O LORD God of Israel, let thy word be verified, which thou hast spoken unto thy servant David."

Modern Corruption

Prayer is treated as the presentation of wishes; Solomon prays God's own promise back to Him and asks for nothing else.

expand to see more

Most instruction on prayer begins with what the pray-er wants and how to ask for it. Solomon at the dedication of the temple — the longest recorded prayer of any Old Testament king, at the high point of Israel's history — asks for one thing: let thy word be verified, which thou spakest unto thy servant David. He is not informing God of a need or negotiating for a favour; he is holding up a promise and asking that it be made good. That is what the Puritans meant by pleading the promises, and it is the difference between prayer that is finally about the one praying and prayer that is finally about God's faithfulness to His own word.

The Genesis use adds the other half. Joseph tells his brothers their words will be verified by an action, not by an assurance, and the verification takes three chapters, a famine, a silver cup and Judah's offer to become a bondman in Benjamin's place. Scripture applies the same standard to professions of faith: shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works. Words are verified by what a man does when the test arrives, and the test is usually the same situation that exposed him the first time.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'aman (H539), to confirm, to be established, to be faithful — the root of amen; dabar (H1697), word; bachan (H974), to test, to try.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'aman (H539) — to confirm, to support, to be faithful or established; 1 Kings 8:26, 2 Chronicles 6:17 — and the root of amen and of faith.

Hebrew bachan (H974) — to examine, to prove, to try as metal; Genesis 42:20, so shall your words be proved.

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — word, promise, matter; the thing Solomon asks to be verified.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant faithfulness; the ground on which any promise is pleaded.

Greek bebaioo (G950) — to confirm, to make firm; 2 Corinthians 1:20, all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen.

Usage

"“Let thy word, I pray thee, be verified” — the whole of Solomon's request."

"“So shall your words be verified” — and it took three chapters."

"“Let thy word be verified, which thou hast spoken unto thy servant David”."
